title: Launch HN: ProvenMetal (YC S26) 在数天内交付电路板，而不是数周
text:
嗨，HN，我们是 Will 和 Johnny，来自 ProvenMetal（https://provenmetal.com）。你给我们发送设计文件或规格，我们在数天内为你提供国内组装的电路板。

2000 年美国生产了全球 30% 的 PCB，现在只生产 4%。中国制造商以 55% 的全球产量完全主导了这个领域。

如今，对国内 PCB 供应链的需求比以往任何时候都更高，但基础设施在过去 20 年里一直在瓦解。剩下的主要是小型家族经营的制造商（CM），自 2000 年代初以来基本以相同的劳动密集型方式运营。

当你通过 CM 下订单时，通常需要数天时间才能收到报价并完成可制造性设计审查，然后你必须自己采购所有元件（最难的部分）和裸板，然后等待数天到数周不等的组装和测试时间。

我们最初是在车库里用消费级专业设备（NeoDen YY1、Glenbrook X 射线、焊锡膏模板和手动返修台）组装电路板。我们相信，通过拥有制造过程，我们可以将所有前端的自动化转向内部。但事实是……在车库里用消费级专业设备制造电路板需要大量时间。突然之间，我们 90% 的时间都花在了组装电路板上，而不是发展业务。我们完全受限于产能，那些花哨的软件自动化在低产量时并不是真正的瓶颈。

然后我们从琐事中抬起头来，退后一步，意识到我们一直在试图解决错误的瓶颈。

这些制造商擅长制造，却在前端（报价、DFM 审查和元件采购）方面非常糟糕。当你审视整个过程时，你会发现组装不是瓶颈。所以我们停止了在这个阶段试图解决我们无法解决的问题。

我们衡量了瓶颈，并确定了我们现在最有能力解决的瓶颈。

当客户想要国内制造的电路板时，这不是一个简单的过程。我们正在通过前端自动化使这个过程变得简单。客户给我们设计文件，我们自动采购元件，并协调裸板制造和组装厂商，以在非常紧凑的循环中完成报价、设计审查和制造。

我们如何解决元件采购问题（没有元件就无法组装电路板！）：当用户向我们下订单时，我们的系统会自动从美国和海外分销商采购他们的物料清单。然而，当我们在设计过程中与客户合作时，我们的插件会与 KiCAD 和 Altium 交互，将 BOM 发送到我们的订购平台，这使我们能够在布局最终确定之前自动采购元件。

KiCAD 插件：（https://github.com/proven-metal/provenmetal-kicad）

Altium 插件：（https://github.com/proven-metal/provenmetal-altium）

这使我们能够提前订购长交期元件，在元件缺货时建议替代方案，并解决流程中最大的瓶颈。我们在旧金山总部存储元件，然后配套电路板并通过我们的网络进行路由。我们还为长交期元件提供长期存储。

我们如何解决无休止的邮件问题：每个制造商都想要相同的信息，但形式不同。通常需要数天的来回邮件才能明确。我们在为每个制造商建立一个档案，并发送符合其要求的订单。这听起来可能微不足道，但它消除了大多数订单上多日的往返时间，在快速周转的构建中，这占了相当大的时间份额。

如何解决设计审查：每个制造商都有单独的能力表，因此我们有一个启发式工具，由 Fable 5 用来检查电路板的 DFM 问题。我们正在为端到端 PCB 制造构建一个简化的流程，但这足以解决供应链问题吗？绝对不够。产能才是问题，再多的智能软件也无法解决它。我们今天正在从系统中提取真正的空闲时间，这种 slack 是有限的，在一定产量下，唯一剩下的办法就是增加物理产能。我们认为这就是方向。

我们根据订单复杂性按订单价值收取简单的利润，报价明细完全透明。我们在不到一周的时间内接到了第一个付费订单，并在 6 周内完成了约 11 个订单共 7 万美元的交易。

我们非常感兴趣你的意见。我们在一个到处都有问题的领域工作，关于解决哪些问题以及如何解决这些问题，我们不断被拉向各个疯狂的方向。你知道什么我们可以学习的吗？
comment:
祝你好运！你可以提供的一个有价值的差异化是信贷额度。如果你在价格上无法获胜，你可以帮助客户在现金转换周期上获胜。

我做硬件已经 20 年了。我最高产量的产品是 Flybrix，一个由 Seeed 和 UniPrecision 在中国生产、由 Sparqtron 在加州 Fremont 生产的 LEGO 无人机套件。我很乐意与你们合作进行 v2 重启：Flybrix Swarmz，因为每个美国高中都需要一个无人机蜂群。

除此之外，我与许多国内供应商合作过，也构建过 ITAR 控制的产品。即使不拥有生产能力，如果你能在制造上提供 Net 90 信用，并为元件提供信贷——超越现有的 DigiKey、Arrow、Mouser 和供应商信贷额度——那么我可以构建产品并获得报酬，而无需预先承担所有资本风险。

保理很贵，尤其是针对采购订单而不是发票的保理，而且我不知道有任何人仅根据 SBIR 奖项提供营运资金信贷。

信贷才是让香料流动的关键。
哇。听起来是一个超级有趣的产品。还没有考虑过信贷额度，但对一些高客单价客户来说肯定会有价值。

我们目前使用一家美国小型合同制造商，基本按你说的那样运作。交货时间很糟糕（7 周以上，不是 7 天），这是一个主要问题，但我们继续使用他们的原因恰好有两个：

1. 信贷额度——我们在收到测试产品之前不会被收费。 2. 愿意处理高混合、低产量的产品。一个产品线示例：在 2 个 PCB 上有 12 个 SKU，95-98% 的元件是共用的，一组元件（我们不需要预先付费），报价为构建 SKU 1 的 20 个、SKU 2 的 50 个、SKU 3 的 10 个等，而不收取 2-3 倍的价格。

我们在研究/测试设备/国防领域制造，我听说过类似的小型硬件公司的类似情况。

我的信贷额度经验并不是独一无二的，我认为这是美国商业的一个被低估的优势之一：我们拥有足够稳定的商业法律系统，使得经济中的很大一部分可以基于信贷运行。

我一直认为有一个很大的机会，通过预先选择过剩零件的销售来为元件融资。对于一个 Q4 销量很大的消费电子产品，我的年度销售完全取决于我在 10 月 19 日之前能订购多少芯片，但我每年 1 月会有过剩库存，因为东西是以不同尺寸的卷轴出售的。
好的，公平的观点。2. 是我们现在关注的重点，然后我们可能会随着时间的推移增加 1。
Sad to see the Lego drone sold out, hope you get that reboot going!
Credit based on a SBIR is a great idea. Seems like something the Small Business Administration should offer.

知道定价会是什么样子吗？你在页面上特别提到无人机和国防行业，这让我觉得这是非常昂贵的。

我最近给在中国做 PCB 询价，非常便宜。我的设计不复杂，几个 IC，几个连接器，还有十几个无源器件。PCB 制造、元件和焊接/组装每块板总共大约 10-20 美元，而且没有任何数量折扣。在美国，光是元件就要那么多钱，我怀疑你外包的那些公司也对小订单不感兴趣，所以他们可能会报很高的设置费（看起来你目前的平均订单约为 7000 美元）。

基本上把这个服务想成 Crye 裤子等在美国国内制造的原因。但应用于电路板。

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berry_Amendment

更具体地说，有许多新的大范围禁令，禁止进口中国大陆制造的无人机组件，如飞控板、ESC、电源分配板、电机。

"Blue UAS" 的定义早于现任美国政府行政分支最近做出的更具侵略性的变化，但仍然相关：

https://www.google.com/search?client=firefox-b-d&q=blue+UAS+...
这正是我们的初始市场。我们意识到你不能长时间击败中国，那么在那段时间你做什么呢？在你有结构性优势的地方满足需求。

我能问你在与任何既定的美国国防导向电子公司合作吗，这些公司在审计/记录元件来源和整个 BOM 的保管链方面走得更远？有美国制造的电路板是很好的，但如果某个微控制器型号只有一两个来源，而它们在中国大陆，这是一个必须记录在某处的已知警告……或者如果同一产品在更高价格下来自不同地点。那种事情。

我能提供的一个例子是澳大利亚的 ESC 制造商 APD。他们销售用于商业电影/拍摄行业（携带 RED Komodo 尺寸摄像头的大型四轴和同轴八轴飞行器）的 ESC，但也用于国防……
还没有与他们合作过，但这是我们的目标之一。我们生成文档以追溯供应链中的所有元件。在元件确实只在中国有货的情况下，我们清楚地说明这一点。

Yes, pricing is much higher than China over here, mainly due to the non-existent support for high-mix low-volume work. NRE adds a lot, and so the prices are high right now. This is why we need to own the stack, optimize for high-mix, and drive down costs over time. It will take a lot of work.

It's also the immense know-how Chinese manufacturers have accumulated at this point. For a 5-piece hobby order $25 shipped, I got feedback confirming a wrong-looking part of my design before they printed.
And their ability to pollute without regard for life or the future.
[dead]
Which manufacturer was that?
JLCPCB.

I'll hijack this point to talk about robotics - I think we agree 1) It's not ideal for China to control production for _all_ of the things we use here.

2) What they already are good at they'll continue to improve at, because of domain knowledge & ecosystem

3) The reason they are ahead in the first place is labor cost & the QOL workers will tolerate (and intentional government investment)

4) The only way around this is for the US to invest into robotics (labor) & subsidize american manufacturing (ecosystem)

> The reason they are ahead in the first place is labor cost & the QOL workers will tolerate

That hasn't been accurate in a decade. Chinese labor costs have been higher than Mexico since before Covid. They have more efficient firms, business processes and so much more. The parenthesized "(and intentional government investment)" is related to how they developed nimbler systems, but ignores the totality of industrial policy.
In this case specifically they also have a huge amount of automation and process learnings from being around for 20+ years.
They also have a pretty organised society and a strong focus on education, so given money they will run with it a long way.

I totally agree that we need to reinvigorate manufacturing in the US and that it’s going to take the government (federal level) to make this happen. But for some reason we’d rather give those tax dollars to billionaires and elect incompetents like the current president.

Agreed completely. The recent bans are one way of doing this but not the most sustainable long term at all.

We have two options, give up and allow China to control all production, or start the hard battle to improve manufacturing here.

It will definitely be expensive, and if you raised any eyebrow, you will get “made in the US” remarks immediately. Regarding “drone”, it’s a buzz word, in the past two years everyone is piggy backing on it like how all industries did with “crypto” years ago and “cyber” years before, or others with “AI” in software world now, “drone” is the word for hardware related, any new product or startup that has hardware involved, you will see this word quickly. I hate it and I hate how they ruined this amazing hobby with all their corporate defense BS, but oh well.

It's important to focus on where real innovation in the space is happening, and to me that's in drones. Some of the hype is overstated but drones are the new additions to conflict, and they're clearly not going away.

A lot of the hype is overstated, and I have been in drone world since 2014, but because of the weaponization of them and the global atmosphere of militarization, there’s a LOT of money pouring in now, so everyone wants a piece of that cake. In reality, their (the fpv ones specifically) success rates are around 1/10, but only the successful ones are shown for obvious reasons.

Also, I did mention back in 2020 that drones are the only practical type of robotics compared to others, although I meant for good purposes not how they are used right now.
Yes even if the success rates are 1/10 they are still causing serious damage for their cost in modern conflicts. Agreed that the hype is overstated.
And if the success rate is 1/10 but the cost is 1/100… that’s still a win as far as the war chest is concerned.

One of your major choices is how much you want to specialise, vs be a general service. I expect you're in the phase of discovering that. Now, with the disclaimer I'm just a random guy who knows not-much about business - and is just a small hobbyist electronics guy - it seems clear that your stiffest headwinds are at General Service. I would be leery of how much success you'd have there, because general PCB service is something the world has A LOT MORE of than it had 10 years ago, and the economics are on balance unfavourable to you.

But to (very slightly!) paraphase you, you think it's important to focus on drones/defense and other nationalist areas where the future is canted toward you, and while that is not an area I'd enjoy working in myself (no personal judgement on you, but I'd rather spend my life doing things other than conflict and war), that is clearly what you know to be your first-rank business chance.

Yes I agree. If it turns out that there is not enough demand to service in defense, we can use the optimizations found from the defense market to take a stab at the general market. It doesn't make sense to start with that off the bat.
Still remember when people mostly referred to them as "quadcopters."

This is essentially the problem with a lot of US fabs. Many exist only as a technicality for the defense industry to make things domestically. This means they get the "$1,000 hammer" margins. When you approach them for a prototype, they essentially don't want your business.

Drones and defense have nothing to do with expense. It is 100% about getting on the approved vendor list, at which point the prices go up.

It’s not like PCB boards in the defense industry are somehow special, though they probably should be.

> Drones and defense have nothing to do with expense

I would disagree? Look at Helsing, the german manufacturer of loitering munitions, and its direct competitors who are trying hard to get per-unit costs way down. Without even mentioning the myriad of Ukrainian manufacturers who are building cheap and cheerful things under $10,000 per unit (or even under $2500 per unit). There is a very real push within all NATO militaries now to basically copy many of the capabilities the Ukrainians have built in the last 4-5 years.

Not saying that we won't still have lots of huge dollar items and massive programs like the AGM-158 JASSM, but there's a reason why the US paid a company to basically clone the Shahed-136 as the LUCAS at under $50k per unit.
Volume unit costs matter a lot. What matters less is cost during prototyping and development, where speed to iteration becomes way more important.

I absolutely agree, if you have just a few people who are each paid 180k a year sitting around waiting for something to arrive because the low-quantity prototyping vendor is slow, it's not the best use of resources at all. One of the reasons why certain companies spend a lot of money buying their own laser sintering 3D printers for low volume test-fit protoypes in the aerospace industry, or invest in their own small-scale CNC stuff to do similar.
medium to large defence companies tend to have in house board fabs. I worked in one.
yes, what was the utilization like?

20-40% capacity. Reserve available. Turnaround same day on a board (2 layer). Next day 4 layer. Two days exotic (rogers etc). Pick, place, soldered 2 days or delivered to lab immediately after panel cut.

If they had a fast production run in they could extend to 24 hours operation and triple base capacity.

They did a fair bit of TH though which was manually stuffed and wave soldered which could slow stuff down considerably.
Very interesting, I'm wondering if that low-utilization rate justifies the capex of building a line.
It's mostly for security reasons. Both supply chain and secrecy.
Low utilisation would be a good thing as they would value availability to the line very highly.
Yes and no, I could imagine a system where they have on demand capacity with a company like us and pay for that service.

I see what you did there. :-)
Good luck with your venture btw.
